question: What primary structural feature makes mucous membranes more permeable to drugs than the outer skin?

options.A: Thick layer of dead epithelial cells on the surface
options.B: Presence of numerous sweat glands and hair follicles
options.C: High concentration of subcutaneous adipose tissue
options.D: Absence of a thick keratinized stratum corneum layer

explanation: Mucous membranes lack the tough, protective outer layer of dead cells found on standard skin, allowing drug molecules to diffuse across the tissue much faster. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h1)

question: Why is the mucous membrane route frequently chosen over the oral route for patients experiencing severe, continuous vomiting?

options.A: It prevents immediate rejection of the medication through emesis
options.B: It ensures the medication is absorbed exclusively in the stomach
options.C: It guarantees a slower, more prolonged release profile
options.D: It completely eliminates all systemic side effects of the drug

explanation: When a patient cannot keep oral medications down due to vomiting, utilizing alternative surfaces like the rectum or oral mucosa ensures the drug stays in contact with the body long enough to be absorbed. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h1)

question: Where must a nurse place a sublingual medication for proper absorption?

options.B: On top of the tongue surface

explanation: Sublingual medications are designed to dissolve rapidly in the pocket beneath the tongue where mucosal blood supply is dense. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h2)

question: What instruction should a nurse give to a patient prescribed a sublingual tablet?

options.A: Chew the tablet thoroughly to accelerate the systemic absorption process
options.B: Avoid drinking or swallowing saliva until the tablet dissolves completely
options.C: Swallow the medication immediately with a full glass of warm water
options.D: Brush your teeth vigorously right after placing the pill in your mouth

explanation: Swallowing prematurely washes the drug into the gastrointestinal tract, where digestive enzymes and first-pass metabolism can destroy or alter its efficacy. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h2)

question: Where is the correct anatomical site for instilling ophthalmic liquid drops?

options.A: The inner canthus of the eye

explanation: Dropping medication into the conjunctival sac prevents direct corneal trauma and holds the liquid in place for optimal local absorption. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h3)

question: Why is gentle pressure applied to the nasolacrimal duct after administering certain eye drops?

options.A: To prevent the patient from crying during the procedure
options.B: To force the liquid deeper into the inner ear canal
options.C: To minimize unwanted systemic absorption of the drug
options.D: To stimulate blinking and spread the medication faster

explanation: Blocking the tear duct temporarily stops the medication from draining into the nasal cavity and entering systemic circulation, keeping the effect local. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h3)

question: Beyond which anatomical structure must a nurse insert a rectal suppository for proper retention?
explanation: If the suppository is not pushed past the internal anal sphincter, the body's natural peristaltic reflex will expel it. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h4)

question: What is a major pharmacokinetic advantage of rectal drug administration compared to standard oral ingestion?

options.A: It guarantees 100 percent complete absorption every time
options.B: It eliminates any possibility of local rectal irritation
options.C: It can partially bypass first-pass hepatic metabolism
options.D: It completely avoids the need for systemic blood circulation

explanation: Blood drainage from the lower rectum flows directly into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver on the first pass for a portion of the drug dose. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h4)

question: What property allows certain drug molecules to cross mucous membrane barriers rapidly via passive diffusion?
explanation: Lipophilic (lipid-soluble) substances easily pass through the lipid bilayers of epithelial cell membranes without requiring active transport mechanisms. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized advantage of mucous membrane drug administration?

options.A: Usefulness when the patient is unconscious or vomiting
options.B: Avoidance of harsh gastric acids and digestive enzymes
options.C: Rapid systemic onset compared to standard oral tablets
options.D: Guaranteed uniform absorption regardless of local mucus presence

explanation: Excessive mucus, inflammation, or localized pathology can actually impair and make absorption erratic, meaning uniform absorption is never guaranteed. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h5)

question: What is the primary reason a nurse must inspect mucosal tissue before applying a topical medication?

options.A: To calculate the exact body surface area of the patient
options.B: To measure the local pH balance of the epithelial cells
options.C: To check for integrity issues or lesions that alter absorption
options.D: To determine the precise blood pressure of the individual

explanation: Damaged, inflamed, or ulcerated mucosa can absorb drugs too rapidly or cause severe local pain, requiring the nurse to consult the prescriber first. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h6)

question: A patient is prescribed a vaginal cream for a fungal infection. What critical teaching point must the nurse include?

options.A: Continue using the medication for the full prescribed duration even if symptoms resolve
options.B: Double the next dose if you forget to apply the cream the previous evening
options.C: Wash the vaginal vault thoroughly with harsh antibacterial soap daily
options.D: Stop the treatment immediately as soon as itching and discharge stop

explanation: Stopping anti-infective therapy early frequently leads to a recurrence of the infection due to incomplete eradication of the pathogen. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T15#GNS125_U3_T15_h6)
